title: Chaupai Sahib
hookLine: a prayer asking to be kept under the Guru's protecting hand

cards: A child is crossing a busy road. Halfway across, without looking up, the small hand reaches out, and a bigger hand closes around it. Nobody has to say anything.
Grown-ups have their own versions of that moment: a diagnosis, a turbulent flight, a phone call at two in the morning. Sikhs have a prayer built around that reach.
Some say it every day, and some say it again when they're afraid.

teach.b: It's called Chaupai Sahib, by Guru Gobind Singh, from the Dasam Granth. Its full name is often given as Benti Chaupai: benti means a humble request, and chaupai is the verse form, short lines grouped in fours.
Sikhs who keep the five-bani Nitnem recite it in the morning, it's part of the evening Rehras, and it's one of the banis read at the Amrit ceremony. The whole of it is one long request: keep me.
The opening, in paraphrase: protect me, giving me your hand; may the wish of my heart be fulfilled. Let my mind stay at your feet; cherish me as your own. Then the prayer widens.

It asks to be kept from enemies, from harm, from those who would do wrong. It praises the One who creates and sustains everything, who knows each heart from inside. And it keeps returning to that picture of the hand.
What's striking is that it's a request at all.
Its author was the tenth Guru, and Sikh tradition remembers the hardships of his life: his father's execution, and later the deaths of his sons. Yet the prayer has no swagger in it.
It speaks as someone asking to be carried.
Some people expect a prayer for protection to promise that nothing bad will happen. Chaupai doesn't promise that; the Guru's own life didn't look like that.
It asks to be held, to be counted as one of God's own, whatever comes. That's the reach the child makes on the road. Not a guarantee.

how: Many Sikhs recite Chaupai Sahib as part of the morning banis and within Rehras in the evening, and some say it at times of fear, before travel or at a hospital bedside.

o: a promise that nothing bad will happen
a battle hymn sung before going to war
a humble prayer to be held in God's hand

games.q: what's inside Chaupai Sahib — tap the pairs.

s: Chaupai Sahib promises that nothing bad will happen
it asks to be held and kept as God's own, whatever comes.
Chaupai is also part of the evening Rehras
it's said in the morning by many Sikhs and again at dusk.
Chaupai Sahib is in the Guru Granth Sahib
it comes from the Dasam Granth, the collection of writings Sikhs attribute to the tenth Guru.

games.q: you're frightened: a hospital waiting room, bad news coming. what does Chaupai ask for?
o: a guarantee that everything turns out fine.
to be held by God's hand, as one of God's own.
games.why: the prayer asks to be kept and cherished as God's own. tradition remembers its author losing his father and his sons; it's a hand, not a guarantee.

practice: If you can, find Chaupai Sahib in a gutka, online or as a recording, and read or hear its opening lines slowly. If not, sit with your hands open on your knees, palms up, and think of one thing you're carrying that feels too heavy.
If you pray, hold it up in Chaupai's opening request, protect me, giving me your hand; if you don't, just let your open hands hold it for a while.

wordCard.voice: Chaupai Sahib. Guru Gobind Singh's prayer in four-line verses, asking to be kept under God's protecting hand.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: chaupai, a verse form of short lines grouped in fours.

carryVoice: Your line: keep me. A small hand reaching, and a bigger one closing around it. Go gently.

sources.ref: Dasam Granth, Benti Chaupai (opening: hamri karo hath dai rachha)
